content:
A Muslim who prays, prostrates, fasts and gives alms is often taken in the West for a stranger to the religion of Jesus. The Gospels tell a different story. They show Jesus praying in secret, falling on his face before God, fasting forty days, teaching that God is one, giving alms without show and keeping the commandments.

The likeness should not be overstated. The Gospels do not give the form of his prayers or his fasts, and they do not show the five daily prayers or the fast of Ramadan.

This article aims to provide context to that likeness, insha'Allah, in six practices the Gospels record, each set beside the Islamic practice it resembles. In the Quran, Jesus names two of them as commands he received: "He hath ... enjoined on me Prayer and Charity as long as I live" (19:31).[1]

Jesus taught: "When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men ... But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret" (Matthew 6:5 to 6).[2] He practised it: "he withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed" (Luke 5:16).[2]

The Quran condemns the same fault: "So woe to the worshippers Who are neglectful of their prayers, Those who (want but) to be seen (of men)" (107:4 to 6).[1] We set out the times Jesus prayed by night in 4 times Jesus prayed at night or before dawn.

In Gethsemane Jesus "fell on his face, and prayed" (Matthew 26:39).[2] The posture is older than him: "Abram fell on his face" (Genesis 17:3), and Moses and Aaron "fell on their faces" at the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 20:6).[2]

The Quran commands it: "O ye who believe! bow down, prostrate yourselves, and adore your Lord" (22:77).[1] The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The nearest a servant comes to his Lord is when he is prostrating himself."[3] We set out the prostration of Jesus and the prophets in Jesus prostrated in prayer.

"When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward" (Matthew 4:2). He taught: "when you fast, don't be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces, that they may be seen by men to be fasting" (Matthew 6:16).[2]

The Quran ties fasting to the earlier communities: "Fasting is prescribed to you as it was prescribed to those before you, that ye may (learn) self-restraint" (2:183).[1] The Prophet said: "Whoever does not give up false statements (i.e. telling lies), and evil deeds, and speaking bad words to others, Allah is not in need of his (fasting) leaving his food and drink."[4] We set out the fasts of Jesus in did Jesus fast?

Asked for the first commandment, Jesus answered from Deuteronomy: "Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29). To Satan he said: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only" (Matthew 4:10).[2]

The Quran gives his message in the same terms: "It is Allah Who is my Lord and your Lord; then worship Him. This is a Way that is straight" (3:51).[1] Christians hold that the Trinity is one God and not three; Muslims answer that Jesus' own words leave no place for it. We set out the case in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God.

"Be careful that you don't do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them ... when you do merciful deeds, don't let your left hand know what your right hand does" (Matthew 6:1, 3).[2]

The Quran: "If ye disclose (acts of) charity, even so it is well, but if ye conceal them, and make them reach those (really) in need, that is best for you" (2:271).[1] Among the seven whom God will shade on the Day of Judgement, the Prophet named a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand has given.[5] The likeness of wording is close; the shared teaching is that charity is for God and not for an audience.

Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21). His parents took him to Jerusalem for Passover (Luke 2:41 to 42). He went to the synagogue on the Sabbath "as was his custom" (Luke 4:16). He said: "Don't think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfill" (Matthew 5:17).[2]

Muslims do not keep the Sabbath or the Passover, and the Quran explains why: "To each among you have we prescribed a law and an open way" (5:48).[1] What Islam shares with Jesus is obedience to the law God gave, under the prophet who brought it. We set out the Sabbath in Jesus and the Sabbath.

The bottom line

The Gospels record six practices of Jesus that Muslims recognise at once: prayer in secret, prostration, fasting without show, the worship of one God, charity without show and obedience to the commandments. They do not record the five daily prayers or the fast of Ramadan, and the likeness is one of principle.

It is the likeness the Quran leads its readers to expect. The prophets brought one religion of submission to God, and Jesus, in the Quran, names its practice from the cradle: "Prayer and Charity as long as I live" (19:31).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:183; 2:271; 3:51; 5:48; 19:31; 22:77; 107:4 to 6, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Matthew 4:2; 4:10; 5:17; 6:1 to 6; 6:16; 26:39; Mark 12:29; Luke 2:21; 2:41 to 42; 4:16; 5:16; Genesis 17:3; Numbers 20:6 (World English Bible).
  3. Sahih Muslim, Book of Prayers, the report of Abu Hurayra on prostration.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (al-Adab), the report of Abu Hurayra on false speech and fasting.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Call to Prayer, the report of Abu Hurayra on the seven whom God will shade.
